new_statements.quote: Bloomfield reported that “the vowels of [. . . ] odd-numbered” light syllables were reduced, where the count goes from left to right, restarts after long vowels, and ignores the final syllable (Bloomfield 1957:5). The alternating reduction matches the uncontroversial iambic stress pattern common in Ojibwe dialects (Valentine 1994), which places odd-numbered light syllables in the weak branch of the foot. Specifically, the typical Ojibwe dialect has iteratively assigned left-aligned iambs, with otherwise unparseable final syllables placed in a degenerate foot. While syllables with long vowels are always heavy, closed syllables are not.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Piggott 1983 record (classification weight: stress on every long vowel + alternating stress on even-numbered short vowels counting left to right, count restarting after a long vowel). Bowers restates the same generalization in foot terms (left-aligned iterative iambs, long vowels heavy) and adds detail: closed syllables are NOT heavy, the final syllable always heads a (degenerate) foot, person prefixes are in the footing domain, and in modern Odawa the weak vowels are gone (syncope/restructuring) so there is no unstressed-vs-secondary prominence contrast left. No disagreement on placement or type; the paper is silent on which stressed syllable carries main stre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Odawa/Eastern Ojibwe (Nishnaabemwin), like Ojibwe dialects generally, has quantity-sensitive iambic rhythm: iambs are built iteratively from the left edge of the word (person prefixes included in the footing domain); every long vowel is heavy and stressed and the count restarts after it; closed syllables do not count as heavy; among light (short-vowel) syllables the even-numbered ones are stressed and the odd-numbered ones are weak (and in the 1930s were severely reduced, later deleted = syncope); a leftover final syllable forms a degenerate foot and is stressed, so the final syllable is never reduced. The paper does not single out which foot carries main (primary) word stress; it marks all foot heads alike.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All foot heads are marked with an acute; fn.1 (ms p.3): stress is not marked for modern restructured forms 'since with the loss of unstressed syllables, there is no prominence contrast between unstressed and secondarily stressed syllables' -- i.e. in modern Odawa, after syncope removed the weak vowels, the surviving syllables show no unstressed-vs-secondary contrast. No statement locating primary vs secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Closed syllables are not heavy (only long vowels are); the final syllable is exempt from reduction (degenerate final foot); person prefixes are inside the footing domain, producing the historical vowel-zero paradigm alternations; modern speakers (born after the 1930s) have restructured underlying forms (sec. 7.1: /mkIzIn/ 'shoe', prefixes nda-, ndi-, ndo:-) so the grammar no longer needs to 'build and destroy iambic feet' -- the paper argues against a synchronic stress-then-syncope (recapitulationist) analysis of modern Nishnaabemwin.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper treats 'Nishnaabemwin', its collective name for the Odawa (Ottawa, otta1242) and Eastern Ojibwe (east2542) dialects of Ojibwe; the stress pattern is stated for 1930s Nishnaabemwin (Bloomfield's Odawa/Eastern Ojibwe speakers) and as 'common in Ojibwe dialects'; survey participants are modern Odawa/Nishnaabemwin speakers. the copy consulted sits in the east2542 folder and serves both glottocodes; it is the author's accepted manuscript (ms pagination pp.1-46 after a repository cover page), not the CUP typeset pages 187-224.

sources.quote: 'Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. ... In southeastern dialects of Ojibwe [i.e. Ottawa/Eastern Ojibwe], a very prominent rule of weak vowel syncope is resulting in a restructuring of much of the lexicon'. Also p. 288: no phonetic/instrumental study of any Ojibwe variety exists except Valentine 1987 (Berens River, Saulteaux) -- none for Odawa.
